title: A Husband's HIV Result and a Silent Wife
scenario: Dr. Chipo Banda, a physician in Lusaka, diagnosed Joseph, 38, with HIV a month ago. He refuses to tell his wife, Memory, who is also Dr. Banda's patient, now pregnant. Joseph says disclosure would end the marriage and expose him to violence from relatives. Memory continues to have unprotected sex with him and has just come for her antenatal check-up. Local guidelines encourage but do not compel partner notification. Dr. Banda must decide what to do at this visit.
options: Maintain Joseph's confidentiality and continue to press him to disclose, while offering Memory routine HIV testing as part of antenatal care.
Inform Memory directly of her husband's status, giving priority to her health and her unborn child's health over his confidentiality.
Give Joseph a firm short deadline to disclose himself, with support, and tell him she will notify Memory if he does not.
tension: confidentiality vs. protection of a third party
patient trust vs. duty to warn

title: A Pilot With Untreated Epilepsy
scenario: Neurologist Dr. Ravindra Perera in Colombo treats Captain Sanjeewa, an airline pilot who has had two unexplained blackouts in the past year and an abnormal EEG. He refuses to inform his employer or the aviation authority, saying that doing so would end his career and that he'll 'be careful'. He flies passenger jets next week. Dr. Perera knows that medical confidentiality is strongly protected locally, but an air crash could kill hundreds. He must decide what to do.
options: Respect confidentiality, but counsel him strongly to stop flying and seek leave, and document that advice carefully.
Report to the aviation medical authority without his consent, on the basis that the risk to others outweighs confidentiality.
Tell him he has twenty-four hours to self-report and ground himself, after which Dr. Perera will make a confidential report.

title: A Teenager's Pregnancy and a Mother's Phone Call
scenario: School nurse Ayşe Kaya in Izmir has just confirmed that a 15-year-old, Defne, is eight weeks pregnant. Defne begs her not to tell her parents, fearing violence from her father and worrying about being sent away. Minutes later, Defne's mother phones asking whether the nurse has noticed anything, saying she's worried about her daughter's tiredness. School policy requires parental notification when a pupil's health is at risk. Ayşe must decide how to respond to the mother.
options: Tell the mother nothing about the pregnancy, and focus on helping Defne find a safe way to share the news herself.
Disclose the pregnancy to the mother, following school policy, because a minor needs parental involvement in medical decisions.
Tell the mother only that she should talk with Defne about her health, then arrange a supported disclosure meeting with a counsellor.
tension: safety from family violence vs. rules

title: Genetic Risk That Siblings Do Not Know About
scenario: Genetic counsellor Mikael Andersson in Helsinki has confirmed that Elina, 41, carries a BRCA1 mutation. Her sister Kaisa, 38, lives in Canada and was last in touch four years ago after a bitter quarrel. Elina refuses to inform her, saying 'she made her choice'. Kaisa has young children and no knowledge of the family risk. Preventive surgery and surveillance could save her life. Mikael has Kaisa's address from an old record. He must decide whether to act.
options: Respect Elina's refusal, and encourage her to reconsider, accepting that Kaisa may remain unaware.
Write to Kaisa in general terms suggesting she seek genetic advice, without naming Elina, breaching Elina's wishes but not her confidentiality in detail.
Offer to send a neutral letter from the clinic to Kaisa on Elina's behalf, if Elina agrees to the content of the letter.
tension: family estrangement vs. duty to warn

title: A Patient's Confession of a Violent Plan
scenario: Psychologist Dr. Leandro Gutiérrez in Buenos Aires hears his patient Matías, 29, say calmly during a session that he is going to 'make his ex-boss pay' and has bought a knife. Matías was fired last month after a workplace conflict. He has no history of violence, laughs shortly afterwards, and says it was just talk. The clinic's policy is vague. Dr. Gutiérrez knows the ex-boss's name and workplace. He must decide what to do before the session ends.
options: Keep it confidential, and increase the frequency of sessions and ask Matías to hand over the knife as part of a safety plan.
Warn the ex-boss and notify the police, because of the explicit statement and purchase of a weapon.
Arrange an urgent consultation with a colleague or supervisor to assess risk before deciding about any disclosure.
tension: duty to warn vs. therapeutic alliance

title: Son Asks Doctor About a Father's Diagnosis
scenario: Dr. Nikos Karagiannis, a hospitalist in Heraklion, is approached by the grown son of Mr. Stavros, 80, who is in hospital with early cognitive decline and heart failure. The son, who pays for his father's care and manages the farm, demands the full records and wants his father declared unfit to manage property. Mr. Stavros has capacity for most decisions and tells Dr. Karagiannis privately, 'My son wants my land.' Dr. Karagiannis must decide what to share.
options: Share nothing without Mr. Stavros's consent, and tell the son that his father must agree to any disclosure.
Share the essential facts with the son, considering that family members who provide care and funding should be informed.
Offer a joint meeting with father and son where Mr. Stavros decides what is disclosed, and where an independent adviser is present.

title: A Surgeon With a Positive Bloodborne Virus
scenario: Occupational health physician Dr. Beate Hoffmann in Stuttgart learns from routine screening that Dr. Markus, a respected orthopaedic surgeon, has hepatitis B with a high viral load. He refuses to stop operating, saying the risk is negligible with double-gloving and that his patients trust him. Guidelines are not mandatory in her hospital. Dr. Markus is her friend and begs her to keep this secret for a few weeks until his treatment takes effect. Dr. Hoffmann must decide.
options: Keep the information confidential while the surgeon undertakes treatment and restricted practice with extra protective measures.
Report to the hospital medical director, stopping him from performing exposure-prone procedures until his viral load drops.
Persuade him to self-report and step back voluntarily within a day, with her accompanying him to the meeting.

title: A Partner Violence Disclosure With Children Present
scenario: Emergency nurse Faith Mwangi in Mombasa treats Grace, 31, for a broken wrist she says came from a fall. Later, away from her husband, Grace quietly admits he beats her and the children, but begs Faith not to tell anyone because he will kill her if police become involved. Kenyan guidelines require reporting child abuse but leave adult domestic violence to the victim's choice. Two children, aged 4 and 7, are in the waiting room with their father. Faith must decide what to do.
options: Respect Grace's wish, give her safety information and a hotline, and not report to authorities yet.
Report to child protection services because the children appear to be at risk, even if it endangers Grace.
Admit Grace and the children for observation under a pretext, creating time for a safer plan and a social worker to meet them.

title: Reporting a Gunshot Wound Under Fear of Retaliation
scenario: Surgeon Dr. Ahmed Hamdan in Cairo repairs a bullet wound in a young man, Karim, whose friends brought him in at night. Karim refuses to identify who shot him and begs the hospital not to call the police, saying the shooters live on his street and will harm his family. Hospital policy requires reporting all gunshot injuries within 24 hours. The friends say a report would endanger them. Dr. Hamdan has to decide whether to notify the authorities.
options: Follow policy and report as required, informing Karim in advance, and request protective measures for the family.
Delay the report until the family can move to safety, treating Karim confidentially in the meantime.
Treat the case without reporting and record the injury as accidental, to protect the patient and his family from reprisals.

title: Employer Asks About a Worker's Sickness Note
scenario: Occupational GP Dr. Sinead O'Brien in Cork is phoned by the HR manager of a construction firm. The manager says a crane operator, Declan, has been on sick leave for three weeks and asks, 'Is it his back, or is it his mind? We need to know whether to let him near heavy machinery.' Dr. O'Brien knows Declan is being treated for severe depression with suicidal thoughts. Declan has not authorised any disclosure. A site safety officer is also in the room, listening. She must decide how to respond.
options: Decline to give any diagnostic details and say only that she can confirm whether he is fit or unfit for work.
Share enough about his condition to protect others on site, stating that machinery work is inadvisable for now.
Ask Declan for his permission urgently and give nothing until he replies, even though the manager wants an answer today.

title: Confidential Contraception for a Married Woman
scenario: Midwife Rukhsana Begum in Dhaka provides injectable contraception in secret to Shirin, 27, who already has three children and is exhausted. Shirin's husband and mother-in-law believe she is pregnant again and have asked the midwife, who also delivers their grandchildren, to confirm it. The mother-in-law pays the clinic's fees. Rukhsana risks losing her community's trust if the truth emerges or if she lies. She must decide how to respond to the mother-in-law's question.
options: Maintain Shirin's confidentiality and tell the mother-in-law that she cannot discuss any woman's health with others.
Gently deflect with a statement that is technically true, such as 'Shirin is in good health,' avoiding both lies and disclosure.
Encourage Shirin to tell her family herself about her choice, offering to be present to support her at that conversation.

title: Teen's Drug Use Revealed in an Exam Room
scenario: Family doctor Dr. Camille Lefèvre in Lyon examines a 16-year-old, Théo, who tells her he injects ketamine at parties and shares needles. He asks her to prescribe nothing and tell no one. His mother, a close friend of the doctor, sits outside and asks, 'Is everything okay with him?' French rules give minors some confidentiality but also allow disclosure for serious risk. Dr. Lefèvre must decide what to tell his mother.
options: Tell the mother that he is generally well and she should talk with him, while offering Théo harm-reduction help in confidence.
Disclose the injecting to the mother, as the risk of infection, overdose, and addiction is serious for a minor.
Tell Théo that his mother must know and give him the choice to tell her himself in the room, with the doctor's support.

title: A Psychotic Patient's Threat to a Child
scenario: Psychiatric nurse Aroha Rangi in a community mental health team in Rotorua is told by her patient Ihaka, 40, that voices have told him his young nephew is 'possessed' and must be 'cleansed'. Ihaka lives near the nephew's family and sees the child daily. He refuses admission and has refused medication in the past. He appears calm but his thoughts are disorganised. Aroha must decide whether to alert the nephew's parents and the authorities today.
options: Alert the child's parents and the authorities now and begin the process of compulsory assessment for Ihaka.
Maintain confidentiality and increase visits, trying to build trust so that Ihaka agrees to medication voluntarily.
Warn the parents quietly to keep the child away from Ihaka for now, without disclosing the content of his delusions.
tension: duty to protect vs. therapeutic trust

title: Test Results Sent to the Wrong Number
scenario: Laboratory scientist Dr. Karina Bautista in Quezon City realises that an HIV-positive result for a young man, Jericho, was sent by text to a number belonging to a stranger, Mrs. Lim, instead of Jericho's phone. She can see that Mrs. Lim has read the message. Contacting Mrs. Lim could further spread the information but might contain the breach. Jericho has not yet been informed and has a fragile mental state according to his referral. Dr. Bautista must decide what to do.
options: Call Mrs. Lim at once, ask her to delete the message and keep it confidential, then inform Jericho and the data protection officer.
Report the breach to her supervisor and the data protection officer without contacting Mrs. Lim, leaving the response to the hospital.
Contact Jericho first, so he hears the news from the clinic in a supportive manner, before dealing with the error.
tension: privacy breach containment vs. patient's right to hear first

title: Grandfather With Dementia Still Driving
scenario: Geriatric nurse Mehwish Qureshi in Birmingham visits Mr. Rashid, 83, whose family says he got lost driving last week and scratched three cars. Mr. Rashid says driving is his only independence in a suburb with poor transport. The law places a duty on the driver, not the doctor, to inform the licensing authority. His assessment shows moderate cognitive impairment. His daughter asks Mehwish not to take his keys, but a neighbour's child plays on the road. Mehwish must decide on her next step.
options: Respect confidentiality, strongly advise him to stop driving, and offer help with alternative transport.
Notify the licensing authority herself, giving priority to public safety over his independence and privacy.
Arrange a family meeting and a formal driving assessment so the decision is shared and based on evidence.

title: A Janitor Overhears a Diagnosis
scenario: Hospital security guard and trained first-aider Kofi Asare in Accra overhears, while escorting a drunken visitor, two doctors discussing a patient's positive HIV status in an open corridor. The patient is a woman he recognises as a neighbour, who runs a food stall near his home. A colleague later asks Kofi whether he knows who the 'woman with the HIV' is. Kofi feels pressure from friends who rely on this stall. He must decide how to act.
options: Say nothing to anyone, and quietly report the doctors' careless discussion to the hospital's patient-safety office.
Warn his neighbours to be careful about eating at the stall, out of concern for public health, even though this is baseless risk.
Stay silent and take no action, reasoning that it is not his place to intervene in medical matters.
tension: duty of confidentiality for non-clinical staff

title: Insurance Fraud and a Patient's Secret
scenario: Dr. Haruka Sato, a cardiologist in Sapporo, learns from a patient, Mr. Ogawa, that he has hidden a prior heart attack from his life insurer to obtain cheaper cover, and will use Dr. Sato's reports to claim for a bypass. The insurer later asks for an attending physician statement. The patient pleads that his family's survival depends on the payout. Dr. Sato fears that signing an incomplete statement would be dishonest. She must decide how to respond to the insurer.
options: Refuse to complete the statement without the patient's consent and give the insurer no information about the earlier event.
Complete the statement truthfully, including the prior heart attack, since certified forms must be accurate.
Tell Mr. Ogawa she cannot sign a misleading statement, and offer to complete it truthfully only after he has chosen how to proceed.

title: Colleague's Drinking Revealed by a Patient
scenario: Anaesthetic nurse Ingrid Dahl in Bergen is told by a post-operative patient that the surgeon smelled of alcohol at the bedside before the operation. Ingrid had also noticed it once but said nothing. The surgeon, Dr. Halvor, is highly respected and is going through a divorce. The patient's wound is healing well. Ingrid is unsure whether this is an isolated event, and a complaint could end his career. She must decide whether to report it.
options: Report to the clinical director confidentially, treating the possibility of impaired practice as a patient-safety issue.
Speak privately with Dr. Halvor first, offering support and urging him to seek help, and report only if it continues.
Take no action, because the patient had a good outcome and there is no proof that he was impaired during surgery.
tension: uncertain evidence vs. duty to report

title: Police Request for a Patient's Address
scenario: Hospital registrar Priyanka Joshi in Mumbai is approached by two plainclothes policemen asking where a recently discharged patient, Imran, 24, lives. They say they want to question him about a riot. Priyanka knows he was treated for a head injury after being beaten by a mob. He asked staff to keep his presence secret because he fears false arrest. No court order is presented. The officers say refusal will be recorded. Priyanka must decide whether to give his address.
options: Refuse to disclose without a legal order, and offer to pass a message to Imran asking him to contact the police.
Provide the address, since the police are lawful authorities and refusal could harm the hospital.
Consult the hospital's legal officer before replying, delaying the officers while making sure the response is lawful and defensible.
tension: fear of retaliation vs. legal compliance

title: A Patient with Tuberculosis Who Will Not Isolate
scenario: Public health nurse Elena Popescu in Cluj-Napoca visits Vasile, 45, a bus driver with newly diagnosed infectious tuberculosis. He refuses to stop work or tell his employer, afraid of losing his job and being stigmatised. He lives with his elderly mother and works on a busy urban route. Law allows compulsory isolation but it has never been used locally. Elena has the power to notify the employer and the health authority. She must decide what to do.
options: Respect his refusal for now, maintain the visits, and arrange income support and treatment that will make him non-infectious soon.
Notify the health authority and employer to enforce isolation, as the potential spread to passengers justifies breaching confidentiality.
Negotiate a short paid leave with his employer without disclosing the diagnosis, relying on Vasile's authorised agreement to a general 'health leave' request.

title: Photographing a Patient for a Social Media Post
scenario: Junior doctor Dr. Alejandro Cruz in Lima shares, in a private group chat with fellow residents, a photograph of an unusual X-ray showing a swallowed object, with the patient's name visible. A colleague posts the image on a public social media site and it spreads widely. The patient, a well-known local singer, is identified in comments. Dr. Cruz fears dismissal if he admits his role. The hospital's director asks for anyone responsible to speak up. He must decide whether to come forward.
options: Come forward and admit responsibility for the initial sharing, accepting disciplinary consequences, and help limit further spread.
Stay silent, since another colleague made the public post, and the damage cannot be reversed by his confession.
Speak privately to the director's office to report the situation and the chain of sharing without being publicly named.
tension: privacy breach vs. fear of consequences

title: A Girl's Virginity Test Certificate
scenario: Gynaecologist Dr. Nasrin Rahimi in Kabul is asked by the father of a 19-year-old, Parisa, to certify her virginity before her engagement, after rumours spread. Parisa, brought in silently by her mother, says nothing. Examination has no scientific validity, but a refusal might lead the family to take her elsewhere or cause worse harm. Dr. Rahimi has also been told that without a certificate, the engagement and Parisa's safety may be in danger. She must decide how to respond.
options: Refuse to perform the examination or issue any certificate, explaining that it is unscientific and harmful, and offer Parisa private support.
Examine and issue a certificate stating she is a virgin without checking, in order to protect Parisa from the family's anger.
Meet Parisa alone, ask what she wants, and then decide whether to give a statement that avoids false claims about her body.

title: Overheard Plans to Take a Child Abroad
scenario: Paediatric social worker Marta Kowal in Edinburgh hears from a mother, Dilnoza, that she plans to take her seven-year-old, Anvar, to Uzbekistan next week for an arranged marriage of her older cousin, and not to return. The father, divorced from her, has custody rights and has not agreed. Dilnoza confided in Marta only because she is distressed and asks her to say nothing. Marta fears a child abduction, but she may be misreading the situation. She must decide what to do.
options: Respect Dilnoza's trust and keep the conversation confidential, urging her to resolve matters through the courts.
Alert child protection and the father, considering the risk of unlawful removal to outweigh the duty of confidentiality.
Consult her safeguarding lead immediately for advice, and then decide on any disclosure with the facts reviewed.
tension: parental rights vs. trust in therapeutic relationship

title: Disclosing a Stillbirth Cause to a Surrogate
scenario: Fertility doctor Dr. Rina Kapoor in Ahmedabad learns that the commissioning couple's embryo, carried by a surrogate, Sheela, 28, had a genetic abnormality that led to a late miscarriage. The intended parents ask the doctor to tell Sheela it was caused by a 'womb problem' to avoid blame disputes and the cost of further treatment. Sheela is waiting and anxious, thinking she failed. Dr. Kapoor must decide what to tell her.
options: Tell Sheela the truth that the miscarriage was due to an embryo abnormality unrelated to her body.
Follow the couple's request and give the vaguer 'womb problem' explanation, since they are the clients.
Tell her that the loss was not her fault and was due to a medical issue, without detailing its nature, and refer detailed questions to the couple.
tension: honesty to a vulnerable patient vs. client confidentiality

title: A Mandatory Report of Female Genital Cutting
scenario: Paediatrician Dr. Fartun Warsame in Minneapolis examines Hodan, 6, and sees signs that she has recently undergone female genital cutting during a visit abroad. Hodan's parents deny it and are polite and cooperative; the mother cries. State law requires a report to child protective services, which could lead to the family's investigation and, potentially, deportation proceedings for the father. Dr. Warsame is of the same community. She must decide whether to report.
options: File the mandatory report, as the law and the child's interests require, and support the family through the investigation.
Delay the report for a few days while she builds trust with the parents and tries to understand what happened.
Report, but also seek a social worker from the community to be involved early and reduce the chance of devastating consequences for the family.
tension: child protection vs. family and community trust
legal duty vs. potential disproportionate harm
